title: Signs, Excuses, and the Road Back to Egypt
summary: Moses asks what will happen if Israel refuses to believe him, and God gives him three signs: a staff that becomes a snake, a hand made diseased and then healed, and Nile water that will turn to blood. When Moses pleads that he is no speaker and finally asks God to send someone else, God is angry but gives him his brother Aaron as a spokesman. On the road back to Egypt the LORD confronts Moses in a strange night encounter, Zipporah circumcises their son, and the chapter ends with the elders of Israel believing and worshiping.
story: The chapter continues the conversation at the burning bush that began in Exodus 3. God has revealed his name, announced that he has seen Israel's misery, and sent Moses to lead the people out. Moses has already asked who he is to do this and what God's name is; now he asks what happens if no one believes him, and then whether he can simply decline. The answers move the story from the mountain back to Egypt. By the end Moses has his staff, his brother, and a message for Pharaoh that frames everything to come: Israel is God's firstborn son, and if Pharaoh will not release God's son, Pharaoh's own firstborn will die. The plagues and the Passover in chapters 7 to 12 are the working out of those two sentences. The chapter closes on a hopeful note that the next chapter will test hard: the people believe.
historical:
Moses has lived in Midian a long time. Exodus 7:7 makes him eighty when he first stands before Pharaoh, and Stephen's speech in Acts 7:30 counts forty years in the desert before the burning bush. Midian lay mainly east of the Gulf of Aqaba, in what is now northwestern Saudi Arabia, though Midianite herders ranged through the Sinai and the Negev. In verse 19 God tells Moses that the men who wanted him dead are gone, picking up Exodus 2:23, where the king of Egypt died. The text never names that king or the one Moses is about to face, and no Egyptian record mentions Moses. Which pharaohs are meant depends on how the exodus is dated (see the introduction to Exodus). On the earlier date, in the fifteenth century BC, the king who died is usually taken to be Thutmose III (died about 1425 BC) and the pharaoh of the plagues Amenhotep II. On the later date, in the thirteenth century, the usual pairing is Seti I (died about 1279 BC) and Ramesses II. The chapter's message does not hang on the choice, and the narrator's silence about names may be part of the point: in this story the title Pharaoh stands for a power, and the only name that finally matters is the LORD's.

The chapter also shows how Israel was organized under slavery. Moses does not address a crowd. He goes to the elders (verse 29), the heads of families and clans who spoke for the people. Enslaved or not, Israel still had its own leadership, and they are the ones Moses must persuade first.
cultural:
Signs mattered in a world where every court kept specialists in the unseen, and the three chosen here speak to Egypt directly. The rearing cobra, the uraeus, sat on the front of Pharaoh's crown as the emblem of royal and divine power, and many interpreters see the first sign as a claim that the LORD holds that power by the tail. Grabbing a snake by the tail is also a good way to be bitten, so Moses' obedience in verse 4 is a small act of trust. The diseased hand uses the Hebrew term for a range of skin conditions, not only what is now called leprosy (Hansen's disease); in Israel's later law such a condition made a person ritually unclean, unable to take part in worship until restored (Leviticus 13 and 14). The third sign touches the Nile, on which every Egyptian life depended, and previews the first plague.

Two customs frame the end of the chapter. The firstborn son was the family's heir, owed a double share of the inheritance (Deuteronomy 21:17) and carrying the family's future; Pharaoh's firstborn was heir to the throne itself. Circumcision, which God gave Abraham as the sign of the covenant, to be done on the eighth day (Genesis 17:10-14), was not unique to Israel. Egyptians practiced a form of it, and a tomb relief at Saqqara from the Old Kingdom shows the operation. What made it Israel's was its meaning as the mark of belonging to God. Zipporah uses a flint knife, and flint blades were still used for the rite a generation later, when Joshua circumcised the men of Israel at Gilgal (Joshua 5:2).
literary: Exodus 3 and 4 form one long dialogue in which Moses raises five objections: who am I (3:11), what is your name (3:13), what if they do not believe me (4:1), I am not eloquent (4:10), and finally, send someone else (4:13). The first four are questions God answers patiently. The last is a refusal, and it draws God's anger, though even then God gives Moses help rather than a replacement. Key words knit the chapter together. Hand runs through it: the staff in Moses' hand, the hand in the cloak, and the wonders God has put within his power, literally in his hand (verse 21). Mouth runs through verses 10 to 16, where the God who made the human mouth promises to be with Moses' mouth and Aaron's. The chapter is framed by belief. It opens with Moses' fear, “What if they do not believe me” (verse 1), and it closes with the reverse, “and they believed” (verse 31). Between them the brief, puzzling night scene in verses 24 to 26 comes right after the warning about Pharaoh's firstborn. The placement matters: before Moses confronts Egypt over its sons, his own son's life is at stake and is protected by blood.

outline.t: Three signs for a people who may not believe
Moses' last objections and Aaron as spokesman
The return to Egypt and the message about God's firstborn
The night encounter and the bridegroom of blood
Aaron meets Moses, and the elders believe

doctrines.note: The chapter is framed by the question of belief. God does not scorn Israel's need for evidence; he supplies signs so that the people may believe (verses 5, 8, and 9), and at the end they do. Faith in the Old Testament is trust in God's word confirmed by his acts, not a leap in the dark.

“Who makes the mute or the deaf, the sighted or the blind?” (verse 11). God answers Moses' sense of weakness by claiming authority over human capacities themselves. He also announces in advance that he will harden Pharaoh's heart, opening one of the book's great themes: God's rule reaches even into the choices of those who oppose him, while the text still holds Pharaoh responsible for his own.

Israel is God's firstborn son, a covenant bond with a father's claim attached, and circumcision is the covenant sign God gave Abraham. The strange night encounter shows that even Moses stands under the covenant he is sent to announce.

words.note: Aman, in the form used here, to believe or trust. The root has to do with firmness and reliability, and the word amen, a way of saying that something is sure, comes from it. It appears six times in this chapter, from Moses' worry in verse 1 to the climax in verse 31, “and they believed.” To believe is to put one's weight on what God has said and shown.

Ot, a sign: a visible token that points beyond itself. The same word names the rainbow after the flood (Genesis 9:12-13) and circumcision as the mark of the covenant (Genesis 17:11). Here the signs are credentials that show Moses really speaks for the LORD. In the chapters ahead the word describes the plagues, which are signs to Egypt as well as judgments on it.

Chazaq, to be strong or to make strong. When God says in verse 21 that he will harden Pharaoh's heart, the Hebrew means he will strengthen or stiffen it, confirming Pharaoh in the course he is set on. Exodus uses three verbs for Pharaoh's hardening (this one, a verb meaning to make heavy, and one meaning to make hard or stubborn), and it alternates between God hardening Pharaoh and Pharaoh hardening himself. This is the first mention.

Bekhor, firstborn. The firstborn son was his father's heir and pride. By calling Israel “My firstborn son” (verse 22), God claims a father's rights over a people Pharaoh treats as property. The word sets up the whole contest: the last plague will fall on the firstborn of Egypt, and afterward Israel's own firstborn will belong to God (Exodus 13).

christ: God's message to Pharaoh, “Israel is My firstborn son” (verse 22), is one of the Bible's great seeds. Hosea later remembers the exodus in the same terms, “out of Egypt I called My son” (Hosea 11:1), and Matthew applies that line to Jesus, brought back from Egypt as a child (Matthew 2:15). Hosea is looking back to the exodus, not forward, and most interpreters read Matthew's fulfillment language as typological: he is saying that Jesus is the Son in whom Israel's story is lived again and brought to its goal. The threat and rescue of firstborn sons in this chapter also point ahead to the Passover, which the New Testament reads in light of the cross. Moses himself, reluctant and slow of speech, is honored as a faithful servant, and Hebrews sets him beside Jesus: “Moses was faithful as a servant in all God’s house,” but “Christ is faithful as the Son over God’s house” (Hebrews 3:5-6). And the God who asks, “Who gave man his mouth?” (verse 11) is the God whose Son made the crowds say that “He makes even the deaf hear and the mute speak” (Mark 7:37). That last link is thematic rather than predictive, but it is the same God at work.

hard.q: Why does the LORD try to kill Moses right after sending him, and what does Zipporah's act mean?
hard.a:
Verses 24 to 26 are among the most obscure in the Old Testament. The Hebrew says only that the LORD met him and sought to kill him. Most translations, like the BSB, take this to be Moses, though some readers think the one in danger was the son. Zipporah cuts off her son's foreskin and touches his feet with it; the BSB supplies Moses' name, but the Hebrew leaves it open, and some interpreters take feet here as a polite euphemism for the genitals. Her words, “bridegroom of blood,” are explained only by the narrator's note that she was referring to the circumcision.

The most common reading, ancient and modern, is that Moses had failed to circumcise his son, for reasons the text does not give, and that the man sent to lead the covenant people could not do so while neglecting the covenant's sign (Genesis 17:14 says an uncircumcised male has broken the covenant). Zipporah does at once what Moses had left undone, and the threat lifts. Others stress the placement: coming right after the warning that Pharaoh's firstborn will die, the scene shows Moses' own family under the same judgment and spared by blood, a preview of the Passover. Many critical scholars think an older tradition, perhaps one that explained the phrase bridegroom of blood, has been taken up and given this new setting. None of these views settles every detail. What the passage makes plain is that the God who sends Moses is not a tool Moses carries with him. He is holy, and his covenant is not optional even for his chosen servant.

questions: Moses' objections move from honest questions to a flat refusal. Where is the line, in your own life, between bringing God hard questions and looking for a way out of what he has asked?
God answers Moses' sense of inadequacy by pointing to himself rather than praising Moses' abilities (verses 11 and 12). How does that change the way you think about your own weaknesses?
Israel is called God's firstborn son while still enslaved. What does it mean that God names people by who they are to him before their circumstances change?
